system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2148-09-12 09:14:00 to 2148-09-20 11:53:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 2 diabetes, gastroparesis, and recent right toe amputation was admitted for lower abdominal and flank pain, urinary frequency, and nausea, found to be in mild diabetic ketoacidosis. She had elevated blood glucose and an anion gap metabolic acidosis, managed with IV fluids and insulin, with resolution of DKA. Abdominal pain was not clearly linked to infection or obstruction—renal ultrasound was normal, and urinalysis showed no signs of UTI. Pain was managed with acetaminophen and tramadol, and her home diabetes and gastroparesis medications were resumed. Her hemoglobin dropped from 10.5 to 7.5, likely due to hemodilution, with no active bleeding. Chronic leukocytosis persisted but was deemed reactive. She remained stable, with no signs of infection in the foot wound, and was discharged home on her prior regimen with outpatient follow-up for CBC monitoring and diabetes management.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  TOE(S), 2+ VIEW LEFT

INDICATION:  History: ___ with toe bleeding and pain// fracture

TECHNIQUE:  Three views of the left great toe

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS: 

Lucency through the medial aspect of the first metatarsal head is likely
projectional rather than a fracture.  Likely chronic fracture deformity of
distal second metatarsal.  Mild degenerative change of the midfoot.  Mild
degenerative changes great toe MTP joint.  Mineralization is normal.  There
are no erosions.  Vascular calcifications are noted along the dorsal and
plantar aspects of the foot, and along the lateral aspect of the great toe.

IMPRESSION: 

Lucency through the medial aspect of the first metatarsal head is likely
projectional rather than a fracture.  Follow-up radiograph in ___ days could
be obtained for further evaluation if clinically warranted.  No definite acute
fracture identified.

Likely chronic fracture deformity through the neck of the second metatarsal. 
Chronic stress reaction could have similar appearance.  Clinical correlation.

Moderate soft tissue swelling of the great toe and second toe.

EXAMINATION:  ___ DUP EXTEXT BIL (MAP/DVT)

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with unexplained calf pain// calf pain; r/o DVT

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale, color, and spectral Doppler evaluation was performed
on the bilateral lower extremity veins.

COMPARISON:  None.

FINDINGS: 

There is normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation of the bilateral
common femoral, femoral, and popliteal veins. Normal color flow and
compressibility are demonstrated in the tibial and peroneal veins.

There is normal respiratory variation in the common femoral veins bilaterally.

IMPRESSION: 

No evidence of deep venous thrombosis in the right or left lower extremity
veins.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman s/p L hallux partial amputation// post op eval

COMPARISON:  Prior exam is dated ___

FINDINGS: 

AP, lateral, oblique views of the left foot were provided post amputation of
the great toe through the level of the midshaft proximal phalanx.  An
overlying bandage is noted.  Otherwise, no change from prior.

IMPRESSION: 

Post amputation changes at the great toe.

EXAMINATION:  NON-INVASIVE PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL STUDY

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with DM2, s/p partial hallux amputation w
podiatry on L on ___, bleeding was less than expected in OR.// podiatry and
medicine would like to know if there is established evidence of PVD and
degree.she is experiencing some post op pain, so feel free to call floor to
ask how status of patient is before timing study

TECHNIQUE:  Doppler ultrasound and pulse volume recordings were obtained at
multiple levels in both lower extremities

COMPARISON:  ___

FINDINGS: 

On the right side, triphasic Doppler waveforms are seen in the common femoral,
posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis arteries.

On the left side, triphasic Doppler waveforms are seen in the common femoral,
popliteal, posterior tibial arteries.

The right ABI is 1.43 and the left ABI is 1.01.  Pulse volume recordings
demonstrate likely artifactually depressed waveform in the thighs bilaterally,
given normal waveforms in the right calf, mildly abnormal in the right ankle
and metatarsal level.  Pulse volume recordings on the left demonstrate normal
waveforms of the calf and ankle, severely abnormal in the left metatarsal.

IMPRESSION: 

No evidence of flow-limiting stenosis in either lower extremity.

RECOMMENDATION(S):  Normal left ABI with severely abnormal left metatarsal
pulse volume recording which can be consistent with arterial occlusive disease
of the foot.

Right ABI elevated and could be consistent with artifact secondary to arterial
calcification.

Compared to prior, pulse volume  recordings are now severely abnormal at the
left metatarsal level.

EXAMINATION:  US UPPER EXTREMITY, SOFT TISSUE

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with left axillary swollen tender lymph nodes
would like to assess for fluid collection// Axillary abscess?

TECHNIQUE:  Grayscale ultrasound images were obtained of the superficial
tissues of the left axilla.

COMPARISON:  None

FINDINGS: 

Transverse and sagittal images were obtained of the superficial tissues of the
left axilla demonstrate a 1.2 x 0.7 x 1.2 cm hypoechoic lesion with a rim of
vascularity, possibly representing an infected sebaceous or epithelial
inclusion cyst.  There are 2 other tiny foci of hypoechogenicity in the
inferior layer of the dermis, likely representing sweat glands.


IMPRESSION: 

1.2 cm hypoechoic lesion in the left axilla with a rim of vascularity,
possibly representing an infected sebaceous or epithelial inclusion cyst. 
Please note that this lesion is too small to drain.

procedures.long_title: Detachment at Left 1st Toe, Low, Open Approach

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel. I understand you came in with pain in your left big toe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started three days ago. It’s been getting worse, and there’s some bleeding. I didn’t do anything to it—no injury or bug bite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you haven’t picked up your custom diabetic shoes yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was supposed to get them today. I’ve been wearing regular shoes, but they don’t fit well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of the problem. We’ve reviewed your X-ray from earlier this morning. It shows swelling and some changes in the bone, but no clear fracture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the bone infected? My right toe was amputated last time because of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a concern. Podiatry examined you in the ER and saw exposed bone after removing part of the nail. That increases the risk of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Do I need another amputation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not there yet. We’re starting IV antibiotics—cefepime—for now. We’ll monitor closely. You’re also on insulin and fluids to keep your sugars under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My sugars have been high lately. I’ve been using my chest port for IV meds because my veins are bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted the port. It helps with access. We’ll keep using it for antibiotics and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got your Doppler ultrasound results. No blood clots in your legs, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had calf pain, so I’m glad it’s not a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your circulation in the larger arteries looks okay. But we’re still concerned about blood flow to your foot due to diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve decided you’ll need surgery on your toe today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? What kind?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A partial amputation of the left big toe. The bone is exposed and likely infected. Removing the affected part gives it the best chance to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like my right toe… I was hoping to avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But this may prevent a worse infection. The podiatry team will do it shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went well—partial amputation through the middle of the toe bone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts, but I guess that’s expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll manage your pain with tramadol and acetaminophen. We also sent tissue from the toe to the lab to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Results usually take a day. We’re keeping you on IV cefepime for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood cultures came back clean. No bacteria in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But the tissue from your toe did grow Staph aureus, which confirms a bone infection—osteomyelitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The cefepime covers Staph, and we’ll continue it for several weeks, likely through your port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you for a few more days to monitor healing and make sure the infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a vascular study yesterday. Your larger leg arteries are okay, but blood flow to the front of your foot is poor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Arterial calcification from diabetes can cause that. It makes healing slower, which is why we’re being aggressive with treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The amputation site is clean. We’ll focus on antibiotics and protecting your foot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium level is a bit low. It’s common in patients with chronic illness and can be from your medications or fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mildly low, so we’ll monitor it. We may adjust your fluids. It should improve as you get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The wound is healing, and your pain is improving. We’ll switch to oral antibiotics soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I take them at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for several weeks. We’ll coordinate with your home health nurse for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back on your usual insulin—Lantus at night and Humalog before meals. Your sugars are more stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some swelling in your left armpit. Did you feel that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s tender. I thought it was from using crutches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound. It shows a small cyst, possibly infected, but too small to drain. We’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s not spreading, and your antibiotics may help. We’ll check it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making great progress. The armpit cyst is smaller, and your toe is healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow, if all goes well. We’ll arrange for home nursing to help with wound care and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry in one week, and your primary doctor in two weeks. You’ll also need to pick up those diabetic shoes—very important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I don’t want this happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Proper footwear is key. We’ll also check your kidney function and anemia before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on oral antibiotics for six weeks, continue your diabetes and blood pressure meds, and keep the wound clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will stay in for now. Home health will use it for antibiotics. We’ll remove it later when no longer needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my low sodium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s improving. Just keep eating regular meals and stay hydrated. We’ll check it at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cyst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still small and not infected. Watch for redness or swelling. Call your doctor if it changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep checking your feet daily. Even small sores can become serious with diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll call you tomorrow to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be expecting the call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 2 diabetes, neuropathy, gastroparesis, and prior right hallux amputation was admitted for acute left great toe pain and bleeding. She had not yet obtained her custom diabetic shoes. Evaluation revealed exposed bone and soft tissue swelling; imaging showed no acute fracture but chronic changes. She underwent a partial left hallux amputation due to suspected osteomyelitis. Tissue cultures confirmed Staphylococcus aureus infection, and she was treated with IV cefepime, later transitioned to oral antibiotics. Vascular studies showed poor distal foot perfusion consistent with diabetic arterial disease. She developed mild hyponatremia, which improved with supportive care. A small axillary cyst was noted but did not require intervention. She recovered well, with stable diabetes and no signs of systemic infection, and was discharged home with a plan for wound care, six-week antibiotic course, and follow-up with podiatry and primary care.
